content: 1. In high-income settings, having a water supply on the premises is often considered a basic necessity rather than an aspirational goal. Question G-W1 is designed to identify the primary source of water used by a facility for general purposes, such as drinking, washing, hygiene, environmental cleaning, and laundry. This question does not include water used for medical purposes, such as dialysis. If water is sourced from multiple locations, the main source should be recorded. The categories for water sources are based on the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) definitions of improved and unimproved water sources. 2. Question G-W2 asks about the location of the facility's main water supply. Options include on premises, within 500 meters, or 500 meters or further. On premises refers to water sources located within the building or facility grounds, such as a tap or borehole, rather than the original source of the water. 3. Question G-W3 assesses whether water from the main supply is available at the time of the survey. For water to be considered available, it must be accessible at the facility during the survey or questionnaire. This question focuses on real-time availability rather than generalizing about water availability over time, to minimize response bias. 4. Health care facilities require significant volumes of water to meet operational demands, such as 100 liters per delivery and 40–60 liters per inpatient per day. Therefore, having a water supply on the premises is essential to meet these needs. 5. Sanitation in health care facilities must ensure the hygienic separation of human excreta from contact with individuals. Sanitation is also critical for maintaining dignity, human rights, and gender-specific needs, such as privacy and safety for women and girls. Questions G-S1 to G-S6 evaluate the availability and usability of improved toilets for patients and staff, ensuring hygienic separation of waste and upholding dignity and comfort. 6. Certain sanitation technologies are more effective at hygienically separating human excreta from contact. These are classified as improved sanitation facilities by the JMP, while others are labeled as unimproved. Questions G-S1 and G-S2 assess the type (improved or unimproved) and usability of toilets on the premises. 7. Question G-S1 asks about the types of toilets or latrines available for patients, such as flush/pour-flush toilets connected to a sewer, tank, or pit; pit latrines with or without slabs; composting toilets; or other types. If multiple types are present, the most common type in the service area should be selected. 8. Question G-S2 evaluates whether at least one toilet is usable, meaning it is available, functional, and private at the time of the survey. A usable toilet must be accessible, with unlocked doors or keys available, and must not have structural issues such as blockages, cracks, or leaks. Privacy requires lockable doors and no large gaps or holes in the structure. 9. Questions G-S3 to G-S6 gather additional details about toilets, including whether there are staff-dedicated toilets (G-S3), sex-separated or gender-neutral toilets (G-S4), menstrual hygiene facilities (G-S5), and toilets accessible to individuals with limited mobility (G-S6). 10. Toilets for women and girls should include facilities for managing menstrual hygiene, such as a bin with a lid for disposal of menstrual products and access to water and soap in a private space. 11. Toilets accessible to individuals with limited mobility must meet national or local standards. In the absence of such standards, they should have no stairs or steps, handrails for support, doors at least 80 cm wide, and reachable door handles and seats for wheelchair or crutch users. 12. Hand hygiene is a critical component of infection prevention and control in health care facilities, particularly at points of care and toilets. Question G-H1 assesses the availability of functional hand hygiene facilities at points of care, which may include soap and water or alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR). 13. Handwashing facilities at toilets must include soap and water, as ABHR alone is not effective for removing fecal matter. Question G-H2 evaluates whether functional handwashing facilities are available within 5 meters of at least one toilet. 14. Health care waste management is essential to prevent infections and injuries and to avoid public health and environmental consequences. Waste must be segregated into at least three labeled bins for sharps, infectious waste, and non-infectious general waste. These bins should be color-coded, labeled, and not overfilled. 15. Question G-WM1 assesses whether waste is correctly segregated into three labeled bins in consultation areas. Sharps containers must be puncture-proof, and bins for infectious waste must be leak-proof and have lids. 16. Questions G-WM2 and G-WM3 evaluate how facilities treat or dispose of infectious and sharps waste, respectively. Acceptable methods include autoclaving, incineration, burial in a lined, protected pit, or off-site medical waste disposal. Open dumping or burning is not considered adequate. 17. Environmental cleaning is a vital aspect of infection prevention and control. Question G-C1 asks whether cleaning protocols are available, which should include step-by-step techniques for specific tasks and a cleaning schedule specifying responsibilities and frequency. 18. Question G-C2 evaluates whether staff responsible for cleaning have received training. Training should align with the protocols reported in G-C1 and may be delivered through structured plans or programs led by qualified trainers. 19. The 2016 WHO Guidelines recommend infection prevention and control education and training for all staff, regardless of their role or position. Cleaning responsibilities may fall to dedicated cleaning staff, auxiliary staff, or health care providers, particularly in smaller facilities.
